passA.summary: Barr, an investment partner at Amplify, presents results from the 2026 State of AI Engineering survey (1,048 respondents, run in partnership with Notion and Vercel). The data-heavy talk tracks year-over-year shifts: image generation adoption doubled, audio has the highest intent-to-adopt for the second year running, cost has become a first-class engineering constraint that three in four respondents actively manage, and open-weight models augment rather than replace closed models. The headline finding is on agents: 95% of respondents now use them and 89% of those agents have write access, tripling the share of write-enabled agents year over year — while control mechanisms remain primitive human-in-the-loop approvals and permission gating. Evals remain the number one stack challenge for the third consecutive year, though by a shrinking margin, and 96% of respondents report a problem somewhere in their stack. Worth watching if you want a quantitative snapshot of what AI engineers are actually building with, buying versus building, and betting on.
key_points: The survey drew 1,048 respondents and shows AI engineering is a discipline rather than a job title, spanning founders, CTOs, product people, and engineers across company sizes.
For the third year running, respondents skew senior in software but new to AI: over half of those with 10+ years of software experience have three years or less of AI experience.
Image generation saw the biggest year-over-year jump, with respondents building on it doubling from 18% to 36%, while audio has the strongest intent to adopt at 56% (up from 37% last year).
94% use closed models and 45% use open-weight models, but over 90% of open-weight users also use closed models — open weights augment rather than replace.
Open versus closed was a top-three model selection criterion for only 5% of respondents; quality dominates, followed by agentic capabilities and cost, while only one in five named reliability.

Cost has become a first-class engineering constraint: 40% say it regularly shapes how ambitiously they use AI and another 36% say it sometimes does, and cost/token usage is the number two thing monitored in production after quality.

Agent usage roughly doubled to 95%, and write access among agent builders jumped from 52% to 89%, tripling the overall share of write-enabled agents — yet control is still mostly human-in-the-loop approvals and permission gating.
Evals are the number one stack challenge every year the survey has run, but the margin is narrowing and 96% report some stack problem; vibe review remains the most common evaluation method.
Build-vs-buy splits cleanly: inference and model serving is the layer people buy most, while 61% build prompt management themselves and product-logic layers (prompts, RAG, eval) stay in-house.

97% report a net positive organizational effect — chiefly cheaper failure and more experimentation — but over 9 in 10 also report negative downstream effects like erosion of deep technical skills and codebase understanding, and 81% say AI is blurring role boundaries.

notable_quotes.text: Every year, we see that AI engineering is more of a discipline than a job title.
notable_quotes.why: Frames the survey's central definitional finding about who AI engineers are.

notable_quotes.text: Of those with over 10 years of software experience over half have three years or less of AI experience which tracks uh these are very experienced engineers learning a new paradigm in real time.
notable_quotes.why: Reports the experience-skew number that has held for three years running.

notable_quotes.text: Among AI engineers who are not building with audio today, a whopping 56% say they plan to adopt it in the AI applications they build.
notable_quotes.why: The headline intent-to-adopt statistic and the metric the speaker invented for the survey.

notable_quotes.text: The share of respondents using generative AI for images and feeling really good about it doubled from 18% last year to 36% this year.
notable_quotes.why: Quantifies the largest year-over-year modality shift.

notable_quotes.text: What used to feel like an efficient way to generate cursed hands is just increasingly becoming a part of real work.
notable_quotes.why: Memorable framing of image generation crossing the usability threshold.

notable_quotes.text: 94% use closed models. 45% are using openweight models. But here's the thing, you know, openweight models are not replacing closed models for the most part.
notable_quotes.why: Directly takes a side in the open-vs-closed debate with numbers behind it.

notable_quotes.text: despite the airtime of the open versus closed, it's not what drives model choice. It was a top three consideration for only 5% of the respondents.
notable_quotes.why: Contrarian finding that a highly-discussed axis barely matters to practitioners.

notable_quotes.text: one thing that I found very interesting is that reliability is not near the top. Only one in five named reliability.
notable_quotes.why: Surprising result the speaker interprets as reliability becoming a threshold requirement.

notable_quotes.text: it turns out that infinite intelligence still comes with a usagebased bill.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's sharpest line on cost as a constraint.

notable_quotes.text: 40% of respondents say that cost regularly shapes how ambitiously they use AI and another 36% say that it sometimes does.
notable_quotes.why: Core evidence that cost is now a product-shaping engineering constraint.

notable_quotes.text: Last year, 52% of folks building with agents said their agents could actually write data. This year, that number is 89%.
notable_quotes.why: The single biggest year-over-year shift reported in the survey.

notable_quotes.text: Agents are no longer reading, summarizing, drafting. They're taking actions inside of systems.
notable_quotes.why: States the qualitative meaning of the write-access jump.

notable_quotes.text: The top two are human in the loop approvals and gating permissions which are the right instincts but kind of the same toolkit you'd use to manage an intern.
notable_quotes.why: Names the gap between agent capability and agent control tooling.

notable_quotes.text: Nobody has settled the control layer for agents.
notable_quotes.why: A clean, checkable claim about an unsolved infrastructure layer.

notable_quotes.text: when agents fail or when people complain about agents failing to be more precise, it's usually the thinking, not the plumbing.
notable_quotes.why: Locates agent failure modes in reasoning rather than infrastructure.

notable_quotes.text: Every single year that I ask this, the answer, the number one answer is eval.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's titular finding, with multi-year consistency behind it.

notable_quotes.text: 96% of the people in the survey in this room have a problem with the stack. You just can't agree on which one.
notable_quotes.why: Reframes the eval result as a fragmented-pain-points map for builders.

notable_quotes.text: prompt management is the opposite. 61% build it themselves. Um apparently everyone's prompts are special.
notable_quotes.why: Concrete build-vs-buy number with the speaker's editorial read.

notable_quotes.text: The top effect isn't really just speed. It's cheaper failure, more experimentation, more prototypes, more bets. It didn't just make engineers faster, but it made trying things nearly free.
notable_quotes.why: Reframes AI's org-level benefit away from the usual velocity narrative.

notable_quotes.text: today over a third of teams have non-developers shipping features, which was pretty wild to me.
notable_quotes.why: Quantifies how far shipping has decoupled from the engineer role.

notable_quotes.text: 67% expect a leading lab will declare AGI in the next five years. Note the wording. We said will, we asked about the press release, not the achievement.
notable_quotes.why: A carefully-caveated forecast number that is easy to misread without the caveat.

notable_quotes.text: only 9% bet on Transformers being state-of-the-art in 5 years.
notable_quotes.why: Striking long-horizon architectural bet from practitioners.

positions.claim: Open-weight models are augmenting rather than replacing closed models, since over 90% of open-weight users also run closed models.
The open-vs-closed debate gets disproportionate airtime relative to its influence on actual model choice, which is driven by quality, agentic capability, and cost.
Reliability has become a threshold requirement rather than a differentiator, which is why only one in five respondents named it a top-three consideration.
Standardization is happening at the platform and tooling layer, not at the model layer — 87% of teams use more than one model while over half say their orgs are standardizing on fewer AI tools.
Cost is now a first-class engineering constraint, monitored in production like an SLA and second only to quality.
Agent guardrails have not kept pace with agent capability; no one has settled the control layer, and current tooling amounts to intern management.
Agent failures are predominantly reasoning failures — hallucination and losing context mid-task frustrate about two-thirds of respondents — rather than infrastructure failures.
Evals are the number one stack challenge for the third year running, but the lead margin is shrinking as pain points fragment across the stack.
Layers closer to product logic (prompts, RAG, eval) stay in-house while inference and model serving is the clear buy market.
Fine-tuning is a 'not yet' layer — most teams do not do it at all, and those who chose build or buy are not switching.
Cheap code generation carries a real cost in eroded deep technical skills and codebase understanding, reported by over nine in ten respondents as some form of negative downstream effect.
Shipping software is no longer gated on being an engineer, with over a third of teams having non-developers ship features and 17% shipping customer-facing ones.
An AGI declaration by a leading lab within five years is expected by 67% of respondents, but the question measured a press release rather than a technical achievement.
Practitioners are broadly skeptical that Transformers will remain state-of-the-art in five years, with only 9% betting on it.
